video.title: The New Best Way to Make Money Reselling Online?!

summary: Chris Koerner and reseller Shannon Gene discuss buying liquidation inventory and selling it through wholesale deals, online marketplaces, and live auctions. Shannon argues that live selling can make low-cost apparel lots worthwhile by replacing much of the work of photographing and listing items, while he also stresses audience building, freight costs, and starting with small batches. Chris pitches vending machines stocked with mystery packages, and they discuss bin stores, returned goods, reseller software, and collectible card breaks. Many of the earnings figures are examples or estimates rather than verified results.

ideas.business_model: Buy liquidation inventory in bulk and resell by item or pallet.
ideas.customer: Other resellers who cannot take a truckload, screen printers, and retailers wanting low-cost apparel.
ideas.problem: Liquidators need warehouse space and want incoming surplus inventory removed; smaller buyers cannot purchase a full truckload.
ideas.offer: Buy discounted apparel lots, then wholesale individual pieces or pallets to smaller businesses.

pricing.model: Wholesale resale, priced per item or pallet; no fixed schedule stated.

He says some apparel lots may cost less than $1 per item and suggests wholesaling at $2 per item.

acquisition.how: Software can monitor listings, but assessing lots, bidding, and finding wholesale buyers need human judgment.

ideas.name: Live selling liquidation goods
ideas.one_liner: Sell products in rapid live auctions on Whatnot or similar apps, using live demonstrations instead of conventional listing photos.
ideas.business_model: Auction sales of physical goods through live selling platforms.
ideas.customer: Online shoppers who enjoy live auctions and buying demonstrated goods.
ideas.problem: Photographing, listing, and managing individual items can take substantial time, while new sellers need to build an audience and reputation.
ideas.offer: Present products on camera, run short auctions, and pack and ship sold items.

pricing.model: Per-item live auction; the seller sets starting bids and the final price depends on the auction.

price_points.label: Guest's example for a box of apparel.
Example attributed to a seller stream analyzed with WhatNot Spy.

pricing.notes: The examples are not a guaranteed price. The guest says beginners should sell items they already own before buying a truckload.

acquisition_channels.details: Run live shows on Whatnot, TikTok Shop, Poshmark Live, or eBay Live. The guest recommends watching other sellers and enabling notifications for their shows.

quote.text: Go download the whatnot app and start watching people every night and start watching people sell a pair of shoes every 25 seconds, every 30 seconds, over and over.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

acquisition_channels.details: Build followers and a reputation on the selling platform; the guest says this takes time and recommends starting small.

quote.text: You have to build an audience. You have to build a reputation. It's just like e similar to eBay.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

ideas.delivery: A person presents items on camera and runs the auction; sold items are packed and shipped. The guest says the seller may hire a streamer, while the owner handles the operation.
unit_economics_claims: The guest gives an illustrative stream with 200 items sold in an hour at a $6.80 average price.
A separate hypothetical example suggests $5 net per item after inventory, freight, and fees; the exact inputs are unclear.
The guest says the live format replaces much of the time spent taking photos and listing items.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. The guest recommends starting with items already owned rather than buying a truckload.

acquisition.how: A platform can notify followers and surface shows, but building trust and performing live sales require a person.

onboarding.how: Seller account setup and order capture can be guided by platform workflows, with human checks for stock and policy compliance.

delivery.how: The seller or hired host must present the goods live, and people must pack and ship physical orders.

billing.how: The marketplace handles auction payments and transaction records, with occasional human review of fees and disputes.

support.how: Returns, complaints, and disputes often need a person to decide whether to refund or replace an item.

uk_applicability.notes: The live auction format can transfer, but platform availability, fees, shipping, consumer rights, and VAT treatment may differ by market.

risks: A live seller needs to be comfortable presenting products on camera or hire someone who is.
Buying a large inventory before proving demand can leave the seller with unsold stock.
Platform disputes and returns can reduce profit even where a marketplace describes itself as seller-friendly.

ideas.name: Bin store for liquidation goods
ideas.one_liner: Sell liquidation goods in a physical store, reducing prices over successive days to clear stock.
ideas.business_model: Retail sales of returned and surplus goods with markdowns over time.
ideas.customer: Bargain shoppers drawn to changing stock and treasure-hunt shopping.
ideas.problem: Liquidation inventory needs to be cleared quickly, while customers want the chance to find discounted goods.
ideas.offer: Offer a changing selection of liquidation items at lower prices as the selling cycle progresses.

pricing.model: Per-item retail with price reductions by day.
pricing.notes: These are examples of a markdown sequence, not an established price list.

acquisition_channels.details: The guest describes crowds queuing for store opening days and a treasure-hunt experience; he does not state a specific advertising method.

quote.text: They start lining up because you open up on Thursdays or whatever, there's hundreds of people waiting because it's a treasure hunt.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

ideas.delivery: Operate a physical store, receive and replenish liquidation stock, display items, and serve shoppers. The guest describes daily markdowns but not staffing or store procedures.
unit_economics_claims: Example prices decline from $7 per item to $1 as days pass.
The guest says hundreds of people may wait outside a store on an opening day, but does not identify a specific store or date.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; requires physical premises and inventory.

acquisition.how: Online listings can announce stock, but the described customer draw depends on a physical location and opening hours.

onboarding.how: Staff must receive and sort inventory and prepare the store.

delivery.how: People must restock, assist shoppers, and operate a physical retail space.

billing.how: Point-of-sale systems can process transactions and markdowns, with human oversight for stock and pricing.

support.how: Customer questions, complaints, and product issues need in-person staff.

uk_applicability.notes: The bargain-retail model can transfer to the UK, but it depends on local return-goods supply, premises, planning, and consumer rules.

risks: Physical retail requires premises, staffing, stock handling, and frequent replenishment.
Unmanifested liquidation goods may vary widely in quality and value.
Inventory must be marked down to clear, which can reduce margins.

ideas.name: Mystery-package vending machines
ideas.one_liner: Place vending machines containing returned or lost packages in busy venues and sell a mystery-box experience.
ideas.business_model: Sell mystery packages through vending machines, potentially sharing revenue with host venues.
ideas.customer: Shoppers attracted by surprise purchases and the chance of finding a valuable item.
ideas.problem: Returned or lost packages are difficult to resell as known products; a mystery format makes the purchase an entertainment experience.
ideas.offer: Sell packages of unknown contents from machines, with product categories and price tiers displayed.

pricing.model: Per-vend mystery package, with possible multi-buy offers and different price tiers.
pricing.notes: The host and guest brainstormed prices; none are reported as tested.

acquisition_channels.details: The host suggests placing machines in laundromats or near bin stores and splitting revenue with venues. Getting venue agreements would involve local partnership sales.

quote.text: You split the revenue with some places that you sell it. You put them in specific areas like maybe like laundry mats or some kind of place.
quote.speaker: Shannon Gene

ideas.delivery: Acquire a machine and mystery inventory, stock the machine, and replenish it. A machine can accept payments and vend products, but the business owner must maintain stock and equipment.
unit_economics_claims: The host and guest suggest package prices from $10 to $100 and a three-for-$20 offer; these are untested examples.
The guest proposes sharing revenue with host venues but gives no split or machine cost.
ideas.startup_cost: Machine, venue placement, returned packages, and restocking are required; costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: Venue placement requires partnership discussions, likely in person, and permission to install equipment.

onboarding.how: Machine setup and payment configuration may be repeatable, but venue coordination and stocking need human work.

delivery.how: Vending can happen unattended, but people must select, inspect, transport, and replenish inventory and maintain the machine.

billing.how: A cashless vending system could automate payment capture and sales records, with occasional reconciliation.

support.how: A person must handle machine faults, refunds, and customer complaints.

uk_applicability.notes: The vending concept can work in the UK, but venue agreements, machine standards, consumer disclosures, and local sourcing need adapting.

risks: Mystery products can disappoint customers, especially if the value or contents are misleading.
The speakers suggest planting an Xbox to create excitement; doing so without clear disclosure could mislead customers and damage trust.
Machine purchase, insurance, venue revenue share, theft, and restocking costs are not quantified.

warnings.warning: Do not start live selling by buying a truckload. The guest recommends first selling items already owned and learning the format.
Large apparel lots may require extensive sorting and shipping, and the supplier's stated MSRP may not reflect realistic resale value.
Freight and handling can be the largest costs in a liquidation purchase; include them before bidding.
Marketplace sellers will not win every dispute. The guest says a seller may need to refund a buyer and move on.
A marketplace's stated no-return policy does not guarantee that a buyer will not receive a refund after complaining.
Unmanifested customer returns can be chaotic and may contain goods with little resale value.
Planting an Xbox in a mystery machine to create excitement could mislead buyers if the promotion does not clearly explain the odds and contents.
The guest promotes ResellBot and reseller learning groups, and the host promotes TK Owners and a paid mastermind; recommendations and claims may have promotional motives.
